articles.body: For weeks I have been measuring how far my own numbers can see, and the result was not flattering. On my own publishing account the smallest difference one new piece against a small baseline could detect was larger than the largest number I had ever produced. The design was not underpowered. It was aimed where the data never goes. That is easy to say about myself. The harder test is a paper where nobody handed me the ruler, whose authors have never heard of my arithmetic, and where the numbers have to come out of their own tables. I found one in nursing education. The paper "Integrating ChatGPT into nursing education: a randomized trial exploring knowledge, retention, and student perspectives on endotracheal suctioning." BMC Medical Education , 2026.

The desktop opens the project structure first, then a file shows its full source with views for source, full comparison, and changes. Every finding is tied to reproducible evidence, and you confirm the context before you act. Open the structure before the diff When you choose a code folder, the project structure opens first. That ordering matters, because a diff is hard to judge without knowing where the changed files sit and how heavily they are referenced.

The roughly 50-person team behind the AutoGen agent framework and the Fara computer-use agent was folded into Microsoft AI in early September. articles.body: Originally published at omerbinsaleem.com by Omer Bin Saleem (Omer Saleem). Two background agents each sat on one command for about two and a half hours, with no error and no completion notice. Here is the brief rule and the silence check I use now. What changed Every build brief now bans wait loops and rm -rf. Any agent quiet for about 30 minutes gets a timestamp check instead of more waiting. How to do it Know the failure mode. In a background agent, a command that needs a permission prompt, or a blocked foreground sleep, does not fail. It just waits forever. One of my agents stopped on cp ... && rm -rf ... , the other on until ...; do sleep 5; done . Both looked like they were still working.

articles.title: Logout Does Not Necessarily Clear the Browser's Back-Forward Snapshot
articles.excerpt: Logout Does Not Necessarily Clear the Browser's Back-Forward Snapshot A browser's back-forward cache, often called bfcache, can keep an entire page in memory so that Back and Forward navigation feel i…
articles.body: Logout Does Not Necessarily Clear the Browser's Back-Forward Snapshot A browser's back-forward cache, often called bfcache, can keep an entire page in memory so that Back and Forward navigation feel immediate. MDN explains that a page restored from bfcache may not be revalidated with the server. That creates a gap between server-side logout and what a user can still see in the browser interface. The session cookie may be gone while the previously rendered page is restored from local memory. The risk grows with shared devices and sensitive dashboards. A user opens an invoice or account page, signs out, and hands the device to another person. The second person presses Back. If the page is restored from bfcache, the old DOM may appear before the application has checked the session again.

articles.title: How to sign a PDF with a photo of your signature, without printing it
articles.excerpt: The usual way to sign a PDF that someone sent you is to print it, sign the paper, and scan it back, which takes a printer and a scanner for a single line of ink. The other common route, drawing your n…
articles.body: The usual way to sign a PDF that someone sent you is to print it, sign the paper, and scan it back, which takes a printer and a scanner for a single line of ink. The other common route, drawing your name with a trackpad, gives a signature that doesn't look like yours. A third option is a photo: sign a sheet of white paper once, take a picture, and let the PDF editor keep only the ink. The steps below do that in the PDF Editor of the osFoundry desktop app, on an example freelance agreement. Photograph the signature once Sign a plain white sheet with the pen you normally use and take a photo of it in bright, even light. The editor's own hint says the same: use the flash if the room is dim.

articles.title: Vibe-Coded App Security Holes to Close Before Real Users
articles.excerpt: Vibe-coded app security holes are the gaps your AI builder left open while making the app work. Before real users sign up, close four of them: open database tables, secrets in front-end code, auth che…
articles.body: Vibe-coded app security holes are the gaps your AI builder left open while making the app work. Before real users sign up, close four of them: open database tables, secrets in front-end code, auth checks that point the wrong way, and production settings never switched on. The problem: it works, and it is wide open Your app works. You typed what you wanted, the AI tool built it, and it looks right. People can sign up, add details, and pay. So the question is simple: can anyone else read all of it? In June 2026, Symbiotic Security scanned 1,072 vibe-coded apps using Supabase. 98% had at least one flaw, 16% a critical one, and only 26 were clean. On 172, anyone could delete records without signing in; on 39, anyone could read every table.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 7, 1992: NASA launches Mars Global Surveyor, its 1st Mars mission in 20 years at the time, to map the Red Planet like never before
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission, the first Mars mission in 20 years. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 7, 1996, NASA launched its Mars Global Surveyor mission. This was the first mission NASA sent to Mars in almost 20 years! The Mars Global Surveyor spacecraft was an orbiter. It transmitted data from NASA's Mars rovers Sojourner , Spirit and Opportunity back to Earth. The spacecraft also did a lot of its own science. It found surface channels on Mars that appeared to have been created by running water. Mars Global Surveyor looked at the south pole of Mars and saw signs of possible climate change. It also saw a mineral called hematite on Mars. Hematite usually forms in water. NASA then sent its Spirit and Opportunity rovers to look for the hematite, and both rovers found it near their landing sites. Mars Global Surveyor survived much longer than expected.

articles.body: We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission. Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. 15, 2027. The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034.

articles.title: 'I think we will prevail': NASA chief Jared Isaacman on Artemis, China and the new moon race (exclusive)
articles.excerpt: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman during a a Dec. 3, 2025 confirmation hearing. In October of 2026, Isaacman sat down with Space.com to discuss the future of the space agency.
articles.body: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman is serious about launching "big rockets" to the moon every single year for the agency's Artemis program. And the new space race with China is fueling that ambition. "I feel good. I feel like we are certainly on a more achievable path to the lunar surface today than where we were before," Isaacman told Space.com. We recently sat down with the NASA chief to discuss the state of the Artemis program , and, off the bat, he made it clear that he's confident in the U.S. space program following the success of April's Artemis II mission around the moon. In fact, just prior to our conversation, it was announced that Artemis II commander Reid Wiseman will become the new deputy director of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

articles.title: SpaceX launches mystery mission for US Space Force in gorgeous sunset liftoff from California (video, photos)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force from California this evening (Nov. 6). It was the company's 125th liftoff of 2026.
articles.body: SpaceX just launched a classified mission for the U.S. military. A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from California's Vandenberg Space Force Base this evening (Nov. 6) at 7:48 p.m. EST (4:48 p.m. local California time; 0048 GMT on Nov. 7), rising into the sky as the sun sank toward the Pacific. The launch kicked off the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force , which we know little about. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force told us much about USSF-432 beforehand, and we learned tonight; SpaceX cut its webcast off about 10 minutes into the flight, shortly after the Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth for a landing. A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket launches the USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base on Nov. 6, 2026.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.
